Terimycin (spelling?) is our preferred treatment but be sure to ask a professional beekeeper in your area. Proper hygiene when it's found is essential as it's easily transferred from hive to hive. Once again, all infected combs need to be melted down and you can reuse the comb frames so it's not a total loss of equipment. Do use a weed burner blow torch to scorch out the inside of the hive bodies, lids and bottom board to kill the infection. DO NOT allow healthy bees to rob out the honey or access it in any way, so it's a good idea to either put it all under netting or inside a secure truck for transport to your garage or work room. You can use a blow torch type weed burner to heat up a vat of water to melt the combs. For a small hobbiest I would suggest getting a local welder to weld up some plates to make a vertical box big enough to push the frames down individually. You can wear rubber gloves to protect from the hot wax and water as the comb breaks apart and bits float to the top where you can scoop them off with a strainer. Old dark comb will have the husks of hatched out larvae that come apart from the wax. The husks individually are about the size of the inside of the cells. That's mostly what you will be dealing with besides the liquid wax. The water needs to be hot enough to melt the wax quickly but not boiling. Just shy of boiling is fine. If you bring it to a boil the wax tends to break down into a whitish foam and it is hard to reverse that process. You will want to save the wax as it's valuable. If you're not into making candles you can mix the wax with linseed, turpentine and other waxes to make cream for waxing wood handles and any other things made of wood that you wish to protect.

In the fall before really cold weather sets in you need to open each hive and carefully pull out some combs from the middle of the hive taking care to not crush any bees. Then with the sun behind your back inspect the cells for eggs. If you see a nice pattern of eggs and brood larvae spreading out from the middle with the oldest ones in the middle that's a healthy producing queen. If you see most frames have spotty or no eggs then something is wrong with the queen or she's missing. If she's missing and there is no or little brood left and bees have dwindled down you need to shake out the bees in front of the other hives and if there is no honey in the box just take it away for storage until spring. If there is honey in the combs and they are at least a third full of capped honey you can replace empty frames in a stronger hive with the honey combs. One other thing to consider is pollen storage. If a frame is full of cells packed with pollen the bees will be needing it for winter. They won't need as much pollen in the winter but it's not a great idea to store in your shop where it might get damp and moldy. What I'm saying is, the bees are better at protecting a store of pollen than you are. Pollen is what they make bee food from. It's their main protein source and it's used to build their bodies. Consider pollen to be the body building food and honey to be the fuel food. You can also eat the pollen yourself directly from the comb if you are careful to not damage the central part of the comb which is the foundation. Bees easily rebuild the cell walls by a special conversion process of honey to wax. The wax is excreted from the scales on the bottom of the abdomen in small flakes the bees mold into the cell walls with their mandibles.

Drawing out of the wax cells happens mostly in the spring and summer as the weather warms and they have plenty of honey for wax production. If you are really curious to see the wax on the bees just turn a bee upside down and look very closely at the belly scales. Between the scales you can often see the tiny flakes of wax they make.

What To Do With a Hive That Has an Old Queen:

As I described earlier, spotty brood is a sign of an old queen who is nearing her end. She's running out of eggs. Another thing some queens do is start laying unfertilized eggs all over the comb mixed in with fertile eggs. The unfertilized eggs also hatch out and become drone brood. Bees will naturally create larger cells in torn or broken honey comb or around the edges and bottom of older comb. That's normal and to be expected and while working in hives experienced beekeepers often cut off burr comb which is what we refer to comb that's sticking out and causing damage when putting combs back in the hive body. We like the comb to be as uniform and regular with regular sized cells as possible. It's ok on the outer frames to use irregular combs which are almost always going to be filled with honey if it's available. Drone comb to the outside always and good comb to the center. That's a good rule. However, if you see capped over brood cells that are sticking out above the rest of the comb that's a sign of drone larvae. This will not be in a pattern but rather scattered about the regular sized comb cells in a random fashion. Your queen is almost finished and should be found and killed if possible.

Another thing that can happen is the hive loses it's queen somehow and a worker bee takes over egg laying duty. She has no way to lay fertile eggs to create worker bees and can only lay drone eggs. But, she will drop dozens of eggs in the larger drone cells she finds. You can see these drone eggs all over the bottom of a cell quite easily and they will just be there in clusters. Maybe a dozen or so. It's almost impossible to find these worker layers as they look much like a regular worker so you will have to shake out the bees among your other hives and either take the empty boxes away for storage or if it's springtime put a queen excluder on the top of an opened hive and place the box there to be filled with honey if it's spring time and a flow is beginning.

If it's an old queen you have determined by looking at a poor egg laying pattern you can either take the frames out and in bright sunlight look all over the frame for the queen and doing this for all the frames. Tedious I know so you may want an easier way. You can also place an excluder on top of an open hive and blow liberal amounts of smoke down into the top of the hive to drive the bees down and confuse them. Then start shaking the bees from the hive that had the old queen into the empty box and smoke them down through the excluder. The old queen should be left behind. Then you can place the frames back in the box and after giving it another smoke treatment shut the hive. The bees from both hives will sort of mingle together and hopefully the refugee bees you've dumped on the receiving hive will be confused enough by the smoke to not attack their new queen.

Never jostle or roughly treat a hive when doing this as the bees can become agitated. Some beekeepers use a soft brush to sweep bees off of combs rather than shake them off. I prefer just shaking them off with a sharp jerking motion above the hive.

For making new hives I like to take a very strong hive with plenty of brood and carefully take out the brood from the middle of the hive. Look very closely at the bees on the frame to make sure I am not taking the queen and then transfer it to a new hive body. At least two frames of brood that are mostly capped over and one frame of honey and pollen. Then add a caged queen. You can place the new hive right next to the old hive and if you make two divides place a new hive to either side. Or place a the new hive with it's back to the old hive. Another method is to NOT place the cage queen just yet but to wait until sundown and take it about three miles away and place the caged queen box in the hive at that time with a healthy dose of smoke to confuse their senses. This is so the guard bees of the divided hive don't attack the caged queen. Then leave them alone for at least one week. Do NOT disturb as the bees can become agitated and kill their new queen who is unrelated. They can smell this.

As for royal jelly, if you bought it at a health food store, it's fake or heavily adulterated. Of course you didn't like the taste. You can only get the real stuff from a bee supply business and it's used not for human food but to create new queens. It's hellishly expensive in it's pure form. Think of it as about like caviar in price. A queen producer wouldn't be using it to snack on, that's for sure. I only got into one jar in my life time and it was because my Grandfather had an old jar stored in his freezer he forgot about when he quit producing his own queens or a relative had placed it there for safe keeping. I have no idea and wasn't asking. When I discovered it as a teenager I knew right away what it was and started sneaking a half teaspoon of it on days I couldn't resist. I did that over the course of a summer until it was all gone and prayed that Grandpa wouldn't find out or if he did, wouldn't come asking me questions. If he had I would have just hung my head in shame but dang, I couldn't resist.

For storage of empty comb in the off season you can cut up a sheet of half inch exterior grade plywood using the dimensions of the hive body and nail three eighths thick strips of wood the same width of the thickness of your hive body walls around the edges of the plywood. You can use a good food grade paint on these boards and they are considered bottom boards for storing the combs. They can also be used to stack full honey comb prior to extraction. In this way honey that drips off the comb can be scraped up and fed back to the bees or if it's very clean you can just add it to your product. Personally, I feel it can be a bit off putting to use it for food unless it's filtered so I like to feed it back to bees. It's fine to mix it in with extracted honey that gets sent off to a packing plant because they filter all the honey anyway.

And here's another tip my family always practiced. On the long side of the box at the top right above the indentations cut for the hands we always put a cleat nailed on with eight penny galvanized nails. The reason for this was two fold. First, in the field we used a boom with a cradle to pick up using these cleats. For handling the boxes of honey of course we grab on the long ends and when the cleats are wide enough to extend down to the hand holds it provides much easier hold onto the box so you don't drop it. The small hand holds just aren't deep enough for a 80 pound box of honey and the strain is hard on the fingers. With the cleat it's far more comfortable. To nail on the cleats we use a plate of 1/4 inch thick steel we fasten to a home made very sturdy stand made from two by fours screwed together to hold the plate. The plate is cut so it sticks out enough to slide the assembled box over top away from you and then place the cleat. Then we drive the nail in at a slight angle and when it hits the steel it curves back and clenches the inside of the hive body like a hook. Believe me, with four nails that cleat will never come off. They also make a dolly that you can use to move hives that are attached to the bottom board. As for a bottom board for the hive, you use the same 3/8s thick strips of wood but make the bottom board long enough to provide a landing strip and take off area for the bees. Also guard bees like to sit on that area to guard the hive and watch who comes in and goes out. Kind of like armed guards on the entrance checking ID by smell. Lost bees can get in of course but they seem to get hassled and end up begging for a bit. Of course those laden with honey who got mixed up and just want to unload get accepted much quicker than the others. Robber bees who get sniffed out can get attacked if they insist on entering. Somehow bees seem to know who is who and why they are there. In the fall the entrance is also a sad place for drone bees. You'll see worker bees dragging them out by their feet and refusing to give them food. The drones beg and plead to no avail until they die from hunger and you will see starved out drones around the entrance. They've served their purpose, failed to mate and are of no use during winter months. As a child I would kneel by the entrance to observed these miniature dramas playing out. Over and over the drones would try to enter and get hauled out by two or three guard bees who refused to give them honey. Bees landing would ignore their pleas and just go inside to transfer their load to other bees and share honey with workers. During honey flows drones are well fed but do nothing other than fly around waiting for a virgin queen to mate with. The instant they mate their entire body goes into a seizure with the queen kicking them off to find another mate. She'll do that around ten times before she tires of it and returns to her hive. In a short time her pheromone output will increase far above the reigning queen and she will attract her own loyal retinue. When she leaves the hive for a final time she will have already assembled her own government of personal aides, guards, scouts, hive workers and foragers. She will mobilize somewhere above her parent hive while her nation assembles around her and scouts fly ahead searching for a place to claim. Then her retinue will guide her to the new nest and once she lands the entire force will assemble there with her and begin construction of combs. In a couple days there is enough comb for her to begin laying worker eggs.

Imagine how much information must flow back and forth between all these bees to maintain this organization and it's done not with words but signals. The constant touching, feeling, pheromone signals from the queen, and touching from the bees with special dances that provide information on what direction to head to the new home and even how far. If you happen by chance to be near the area where the new hive will be set up only careful observation and deduction will inform you as to what is happening. First you will notice many bees flying at random and making inspections for suitability to build a nest. To a human making casual observation it seems just random bees flying around looking at random things but nothing they do is actually random. Everything has a reason whether it's for food, water, tree gum, pollen or a place to live. Once a habitat is located or a temporary resting spot the scouts will fly back to the main swarm and direct them to the new location by democratic campaigning. When a majority have the strongest message the rest follow bringing the queen with them. Then the entire swarm will be seen drifting toward the new location in a cloud of buzzing bees.

I might add that one of the preparations to leaving the parent hive is when the defectors suddenly begin gorging their storage stomachs with stored honey from their mother hive. So, the new hive doesn't come empty handed as they've already raided the food stores of their mother hive. Remember, they must start building the new hive as soon as they land, unless of course, the following morning the scouts are not happy and go find another more suitable location right away. If that happens, the entire swarm will take to flight early in the day and take their new queen with them. All that will be left is a small smear of wax and a few lumps of white wax left where the swarm camped out for the night. It's for this reason that when a swarm lands in a tree I try to knock it off into a hive body as soon as possible. If you put them in an unused hive body and manage to knock the queen off into the box you can smoke them down a bit away from the top of the box and gently place the lid over them. Place the box on the ground and the rest of the swarm that you didn't capture will soon realize by smell where the queen is and go there for the night. The queen, her retinue and all the workers will realize in a moment what wonderful gift they have received. An empty hive ready for the taking. They will clean up the combs, scrape them down with their jaws, discard any trash and go right to work that same hour. In three days you can return, gently pull out a frame from the center and see a pattern of eggs already laid.

The most worrisome aspect of Africanized bees is their extreme aggressiveness that hampers the beekeeper when trying to carry out normal operations in a bee apiary. Now to the reasons I think these difference exist.

As for European bees they were cultivated and selected for being more docile, generation after generation. Instead of natural selection to select for behaviors that simply helped the bees survive better in natural conditions humans intervened and selected for traits that made the bees more suitable for cultivation and honey gathering. Hives and queens with undesirable aggressiveness were simply not propagated. Over generations of course this led to strains that work well with human activity.

This is not to say that no bees were cultivated on the continent of Africa because this has gone on there as well even if not as extensively as in Europe nor as carefully I think. Many monasteries cultivated hives not just for their honey but also to produce mead as well as the Vikings who enjoyed mead as well. Where grapes for wine could not be cultivated the wine was substituted with mead.

However, predation by subsistence farmers in Africa was the norm. Africans would seek out nests of honey bees and raid the nests, generation after generation leaving only the most aggressive bees that were able to fend off predation by either humans or animals.

So, we have two different cultures, where one culture cared for, cultivated and promoted the more docile and workable honey bee strains while on another continent another culture did not care for naturally selected for destruction the most docile and easily preyed on strains leaving the more aggressive and defensive nests to go on and continue their progeny into the future.

And there you have it. Natural selection playing out to produce to strains with widely different behavior patterns.

Overcrowding is when a hive is plugged out with honey and brood and the owner doesn't put empty boxes on for the bees to store the extra honey in. When this condition happens the bees are triggered to make the larger cells which generally are located on the bottom of a frame. Like a finger hanging down. One thing we like to do to relieve congestion is what we call split supering. Then, we place a queen excluder to keep the queen from coming up into the top box and place it back together. If there's a honey flow on which is usually the case when we do this we add another super on top of the super we brought up. All well and good for the bees but you want the honey so it's much nicer to have the honey up top. That way you can take it off without removing any brood. So, any bees hatching out of the brood you brought up will naturally use the 3/4 or one inch hole you bored into the front of the box. On return they don't have to navigate through the hive or most especially the queen excluder.
